# Transformations and Importance Sampling {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="analysis-importance"}

- [Variance and variation reduction](#variance-and-variation-reduction)
- [Transforming an integral](#transforming-an-integral)
- [Importance sampling](#importance-sampling)

## Variance and variation reduction {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="variance-reduction"}

Suppose

$$
\mu=\Ex[\underbrace{f(\vX)}_{\text{original}}]
   =\Ex[\underbrace{g(\vX)}_{\text{alternative}}],
\qquad \vX\sim\Unif[0,1]^d
$$

For samples $\vX_0,\ldots,\vX_{n-1}$, define two sample means:

\begin{align*}
\hmu_{f,n}&=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(\vX_i),&
\hmu_{g,n}&=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}g(\vX_i)
\end{align*}

Seek an [alternative]{.alert} $g$ that estimates $\mu$ with
better accuracy for the same computational work

- Often, a useful alternative is [flatter]{.alert} across the input space

- May not affect the rate of decay of error, but [decrease the leading constant]{.alert}

---

### Variance reduction

For IID samples, both sample means are unbiased; their MSEs are their variances:

\begin{align*}
\var(\hmu_{f,n})&=\frac{\var\{f(\vX)\}}n,&
\var(\hmu_{g,n})&=\frac{\var\{g(\vX)\}}n
\end{align*}

IID RMSE is [$\Order(n^{-1/2})$]{.alert}

&nbsp;

[Randomized low discrepancy]{.alert} points

- Are individually uniform but dependent: the sample means remain unbiased

- The IID variance formula does not apply

- For sufficiently smooth $f$ or $g$, random scrambling  gives

    - $\var(\hmu_{n})$ nearly [$\Order(n^{-3})$]{.alert}

    - RMSE of nearly [$\Order(n^{-3/2})$]{.alert}

::: {.notes}
Deck 01 showed that accepting some bias can reduce MSE. Here the estimators
are unbiased, so lower estimator variance means lower RMSE.
The rate statement is for nested scrambled nets and sufficiently smooth
integrands, not every randomized low discrepancy method or integrand.
[Owen (1997)]({{< meta papers.owen_1997_scrambled_net_variance.doi_url >}})
provides the variance result. Since the estimator is unbiased, its RMSE is
the square root of its variance.
:::

---

### Variation reduction for low discrepancy sampling

Keep the nodes $P_n=\{\vx_0,\ldots,\vx_{n-1}\}$ fixed, but choose an
equivalent integrand:

$$
\mu=\int_{[0,1]^d}f(\vx)\,\dif\vx
   =\int_{[0,1]^d}g(\vx)\,\dif\vx
$$

For $g\in\mathcal H_K$ and uniform target $F$, the
[worst-case error bound]({{< meta decks.d03.file >}}#worst-case-integration-error) gives

$$
\left|\mu-\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}g(\vx_i)\right|
\le D(P_n,F;K)\norm{g}_{\mathcal H_K}
$$

- The nodes determine discrepancy $D(P_n,F;K)$, which is typically nearly [$\Order(n^{-1})$]{.alert}
- The integrand determines its kernel-dependent variation $\norm{g}_{\mathcal H_K}$

::: {.key-point}
For fixed low discrepancy nodes, seek an equivalent integrand with smaller
variation to tighten the error bound
:::

---

### The Keister example

Consider

$$
\mu=\int_{\reals^d}\cos(\norm{\vt})\exp(-\norm{\vt}^2)\,\dif\vt
$$

For $j=1,\ldots,d$, set $x_j=\Phi(a t_j)$, so
$t_j=\Phi^{-1}(x_j)/a$, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal CDF

Define $\vz(\vx)=(\Phi^{-1}(x_j))_{j=1}^d$. For $0<a\le\sqrt2$:

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Verify by a change of variables that</span>
:::

\begin{align*}
\mu
&=\int_{[0,1]^d}\frac{(2\mpi)^{d/2}}{a^d}
\cos\bigl(\norm{\vz(\vx)}/a\bigr)\,\exp\bigl[-(2-a^2)\norm{\vz(\vx)}^2/(2a^2)\bigr]\,\dif\vx
\end{align*}

Varying $a$ gives a [family]{.alert} of alternative integrands $g_a$ with the
same integral $\mu$; choose $a$ to reduce estimator variance or integrand variation

[Explore the choices of $a$ in the Keister notebook](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH565Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/applications/KeisterExample.ipynb)


## Transforming an integral {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="analysis-importance"}

To approximate $\mu=\int_{\mathcal T}g(\vt)\,\dif \vt$, choose an invertible map

$$
\vt=\psi(\vx),
\qquad \psi:\mathcal X\to\mathcal T,\quad \mathcal X,\mathcal T\subseteq\reals^d
$$

Let $J(\vx;\psi)=\det\{\partial\psi_i/\partial x_j\}_{i,j=1}^d$

If $\vX$ has density $\varrho_{\vX}$, then

\begin{align*}
\mu
&=\int_{\mathcal X}g\bigl(\psi(\vx)\bigr)\abs{J(\vx;\psi)}\,\dif \vx\\
&=\Ex_{\vX\sim\varrho_{\vX}}\!\left[
\frac{g\bigl(\psi(\vX)\bigr)\abs{J(\vX;\psi)}}{\varrho_{\vX}(\vX)}
\right]
\end{align*}

For $\vX\sim\Unif[0,1]^d$, the density in the denominator is one

---

### Transforming a random variable

Let $\vZ$ have proposal density $\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$ and define
$\vX=T(\vZ)$ for an invertible map $T:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal X$

The densities satisfy

\begin{align*}
\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(\vx)
&=\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}\bigl(T^{-1}(\vx)\bigr)
  \left|\det\nabla T^{-1}(\vx)\right|,\\
\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}\bigl(T(\vz)\bigr)
&=\frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(\vz)}
{\left|\det\nabla T(\vz)\right|}
\end{align*}

Therefore

$$
\Ex_{\mathrm{tar}}[f(\vX)]
=\Ex_{\mathrm{prop}}[f\bigl(T(\vZ)\bigr)]
$$

[A change of variables in an integral]{.alert} and [a transformation of a random variable]{.alert} are the same mechanism viewed from opposite directions

---

### Transport makes importance weights constant

For any invertible map $T$,

\begin{align*}
\mu
&=\int f(\vx)\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(\vx)\,\dif \vx\\
&=\Ex_{\mathrm{prop}}\!\left[
f\bigl(T(\vZ)\bigr)
\underbrace{
\frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}\bigl(T(\vZ)\bigr)
\left|\det\nabla T(\vZ)\right|}
{\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(\vZ)}}_{W_T(\vZ)}
\right]
\end{align*}

- [Exact transport]{.alert}: choose $T$ so that $W_T(\vz)=1$ everywhere
- [Importance sampling]{.alert}: choose $T(\vz)=\vz$ and retain the varying
  weight $W_T(\vz)=\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(\vz)/
  \varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(\vz)$

::: {.key-point}
Transport absorbs the density correction into the map

Importance sampling carries the correction as a weight
:::

## Importance sampling {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="importance-sampling"}

Choose a proposal density $\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$ that is positive wherever
$f\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}$ is nonzero:

\begin{align*}
\mu
&=\int f(\vx)\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(\vx)\,\dif \vx\\
&=\Ex_{\vZ\sim\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}}\!\left[
f(\vZ)\frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(\vZ)}
{\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(\vZ)}
\right]
\end{align*}

The ratio $\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}/\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$ is the
[importance weight]{.alert}

For $\vZ_0,\ldots,\vZ_{n-1}\ \IIDsim\ \varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$,

$$
\hmu_{\mathrm{IS},n}
=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(\vZ_i)
\frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(\vZ_i)}
{\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(\vZ_i)}
$$

---

### One proposal, two unbiased estimators

\begin{gather*}
\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(z)=1,
\qquad
\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(x)=2x,
\qquad 0<x,z<1,\\
\mu=\int_0^1 f(x)\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(x)\,\dif x,
\qquad
Z_0,\ldots,Z_{n-1}\ \IIDsim\ \Unif(0,1)
\end{gather*}

| | Exact transport | Importance sampling |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Correction | $T(z)=\sqrt z$ | $w(z)=\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(z)/\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(z)=2z$ |
| Estimator | $\displaystyle \hmu_{\mathrm{T},n}=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f\bigl(\sqrt{Z_i}\bigr)$ | $\displaystyle \hmu_{\mathrm{IS},n}=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}2Z_i f(Z_i)$ |
| Contribution | Unweighted target sample | Weighted proposal sample |

[Deck 02 acceptance–rejection]({{< meta decks.d02.file >}}#acceptance-rejection-choosing-which-proposals-to-keep): same proposal, keep $Z$ with
probability $Z$

::: {.key-point}
Transport changes samples; importance sampling changes contributions
:::

---

### Variance depends on the function

- [Displayed variances]{.alert}: one estimator contribution
- [Sample-mean variances]{.alert}: divide by $n$

| $f(x)$ | $\mu$ | Transport: $\var\!\left[f(\sqrt Z)\right]$ | Importance sampling: $\var[2Zf(Z)]$ | Smaller |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|:---|
| $x$ | $2/3$ | $1/18$ | $16/45$ | transport |
| $1-x$ | $1/3$ | $1/18$ | $1/45$ | importance sampling |

::: {.key-point}
[No universal variance winner]{.alert}

Target samples $\longrightarrow$ ordinary averages for every $f$

Weighted proposal $\longrightarrow$ better or worse for a particular $f$
:::

---

### Brownian motion with drift

Positive option payoffs may be rare under a discretized Brownian path

Let $\vX\sim\Norm(\vzero,\mSigma)$ with $\Sigma_{jk}=\min(t_j,t_k)$ and
target density $\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}$

Use the proposal $\Norm(\va,\mSigma)$ with density
$\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$ and

$$
\va=\theta(t_1,\ldots,t_d)^\mathsf T
$$

The likelihood ratio simplifies to

$$
\frac{\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(\vx)}{\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(\vx)}
=\exp\!\left(-\theta x_d+\frac{\theta^2t_d}{2}\right)
$$

- Drift makes positive payoffs more common
- Importance weights compensate to preserve the target expectation
- A good drift can [reduce estimator variance]{.alert}

[Asian option variance-reduction notebook](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH565Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/performance/AsianOptionVarianceReduction.ipynb)


## Choosing a transformation {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="analysis-importance"}

- Variable transformation and importance sampling are intertwined
- The sampling density changes the variance of the sample mean
- Require
  - a finite Jacobian determinant
  - a proposal density that does not vanish where the integrand is nonzero
- Pilot samples can guide the choice of transformation or proposal

::: {.key-point}
Place more samples where the [magnitude of the integrand times the target density]{.alert} is large, without creating extreme weights
:::

- [Practical control-variate choices](#practical-control-variate-choices)

- [Density of a sum of uniforms](#density-of-a-sum-of-uniforms)

## Control variates {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="variance-reduction"}

Let $\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_m$ have known zero means

For any coefficients $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m$,

$$
\mu=\Ex[f(\vX)]
=\Ex\!\left[f(\vX)-\sum_{j=1}^m\beta_j\eta_j(\vX)\right]
$$

The estimator

$$
\hmu_{\mathrm{CV},n}
=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\left[f(\vX_i)-\sum_{j=1}^m\beta_j\eta_j(\vX_i)\right]
$$

is unbiased for fixed $\vbeta$

Choose $\vbeta$ to make

$$
\var\!\left[f(\vX)-\sum_{j=1}^m\beta_j\eta_j(\vX)\right]
$$

as small as possible

## Choosing coefficients by least squares {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="variance-linear-algebra"}

Center the response and control values:

\begin{align*}
y_i&=f(\vx_i)-\overline{f},&
H_{ij}&=\eta_j(\vx_i)-\overline{\eta}_j
\end{align*}

Then

$$
\hvbeta=\argmin_{\vb}\norm{\vy-\mH\vb}^2
$$

When $\mH^\mathsf T\mH$ is nonsingular,

$$
\hvbeta=(\mH^\mathsf T\mH)^{-1}\mH^\mathsf T\vy
$$

The residual is orthogonal to the column space of $\mH$, so least squares removes the component of $f$ explained by the controls

## Practical control-variate choices {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="variance-reduction"}

- Good controls are inexpensive, have known means, and are strongly related to $f$
- More controls can reduce the sample size needed for a target accuracy
- Poor controls may increase computation without reducing variance
- For IID sampling, least squares targets variance reduction
- For low discrepancy sampling, choose coefficients to reduce [variation]{.alert}, not sampling variance

::: {.key-point}
A control variate turns [known expectations]{.alert} into information about an unknown expectation
:::

## Conditional Monte Carlo {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="variance-probability"}

Recall the [laws of total expectation and variance]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#laws-of-total-expectation-and-variance)

\begin{align*}
\Ex(Y)&=\Ex_Z\{\Ex(Y\mid Z)\},\\
\var(Y)&=\Ex_Z\{\var(Y\mid Z)\}+\var_Z\{\Ex(Y\mid Z)\}
\end{align*}

Therefore

$$
\var_Z\{\Ex(Y\mid Z)\}\le\var(Y)
$$

If $Y=f(X_1,\ldots,X_d)$ and

$$
g(\vX_{2:d})=\Ex(Y\mid \vX_{2:d})
$$

is analytic, estimate $\mu$ by sampling $g(\vX_{2:d})$ instead of $Y$

[Analytically averaging over part of the randomness reduces variance]{.alert}

## Conditional density estimation {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="density-estimation"}

Let $Y=f(\vX)$ with $\vX\sim\Unif[0,1]^d$

Suppose $f$ is increasing in $x_1$ and

$$
y=f(x_1,\vx_{2:d})\iff x_1=g(y;\vx_{2:d})
$$

Then

\begin{align*}
F_{Y\mid \vX_{2:d}}(y\mid \vx_{2:d})
&=\Prob\{X_1\le g(y;\vx_{2:d})\}\\
&=g(y;\vx_{2:d}),\\
\varrho_Y(y)
&=\int_{[0,1]^{d-1}}\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}(y;\vx_{2:d})\,\dif\vx_{2:d}
\end{align*}

Thus a density value becomes an [expectation of a conditional density]{.alert}

## Density of a sum of uniforms {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="density-estimation"}

Let

$$
Y=\gamma_1X_1+\cdots+\gamma_dX_d,
\qquad \vX\sim\Unif[0,1]^d,
\qquad \gamma_j>0
$$

Solving for $x_1$ gives

$$
g(y;\vx_{2:d})=\frac{y-\sum_{j=2}^d\gamma_jx_j}{\gamma_1}
$$

when $\sum_{j=2}^d\gamma_jx_j\le y\le\gamma_1+\sum_{j=2}^d\gamma_jx_j$

Hence

$$
\varrho_Y(y)=\Ex\!\left[
\frac1{\gamma_1}\indic\!\left{
\sum_{j=2}^d\gamma_jX_j\le y\le
\gamma_1+\sum_{j=2}^d\gamma_jX_j
\right}\right]
$$

[Conditional Monte Carlo notebook](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH565Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/sampling/ConditionalMonteCarlo.ipynb)

- [Antithetic sampling](#antithetic-sampling)
- [Constructing an antithetic variate](#constructing-an-antithetic-variate)
- [IID variance comparison](#iid-variance-comparison)

## Antithetic sampling {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="variance-probability"}

If $T(\vX)$ has the same distribution as $\vX$, pair $f(\vX_i)$ with
$f\bigl(T(\vX_i)\bigr)$:

$$
\hmu_{\mathrm{Anti},n}
=\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\left[f(\vX_i)+f\bigl(T(\vX_i)\bigr)\right]
$$

Examples:

\begin{align*}
T(\vX)&=\vone-\vX,& \vX&\sim\Unif[0,1]^d,\\
T(\vX)&=-\vX,& \vX&\sim\Norm(\vzero,\mSigma)
\end{align*}

Although $\vX_i$ and $T(\vX_i)$ are dependent, the pairs are independent across $i$

The variance is

$$
\var(\hmu_{\mathrm{Anti},n})
=\frac{\var\{f(\vX)\}}{2n}
\left[1+\corr\{f(\vX),f(T(\vX))\}\right]
$$

Antithetic sampling helps when the paired function values are [negatively correlated]{.alert}

## Constructing an antithetic variate {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="random-generation"}

If $X$ has continuous CDF $F$, then

\begin{gather*}
U=F(X)\sim\Unif[0,1],\\
1-U\sim\Unif[0,1],\\
T(X)=F^{-1}\bigl(1-F(X)\bigr)\sim F
\end{gather*}

For a symmetric distribution, this often reduces to reflection about the center

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>For which monotone functions $f$ does $f(X)$ become negatively correlated
with $f\bigl(T(X)\bigr)$?</span>
:::

## IID variance comparison {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="variance-probability"}

Let $\vX$ and $\vZ$ have target density $\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}$ and proposal
density $\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}$, respectively

Compare $n$ evaluations of $f$

| Method | Contribution | Estimator variance for $n$ evaluations of $f$ |
|:----|:---|:----|
| Direct IID | $f(\vX)$ | $\var(f(\vX))/n$ |
| Exact transport, $\psi(\vZ) \stackrel{d}{=} \vX$ | $f\bigl(\psi(\vZ)\bigr)$ | $\var(f(\vX))/n$ |
| Importance sampling, $w(\vz)=\varrho_{\mathrm{tar}}(\vz)/\varrho_{\mathrm{prop}}(\vz)$ | $w(\vZ)f(\vZ)$ | $\var\{w(\vZ)f(\vZ)\}/n$ |
| Control variate | $f(\vX)-\beta\{h(\vX)-\eta\}$ | $\var\{f(\vX)-\beta[h(\vX)-\eta]\}/n$ |
| $n/2$ Antithetic pairs <br>$A(\vX) \stackrel{d}{=} \vX$ | $\{f(\vX)+f(A(\vX))\}/2$ | $\var(f(\vX))(1+\rho)/n$ <br>$\rho=\corr\{f(\vX),f(A(\vX))\}$|

$\eta=\Ex\{h(\vX)\}$; $\beta$ is fixed or from an independent pilot;
antithetic sampling requires even $n$

---

### Beyond the IID variance formulas

- Map, weight, and control calculations add work beyond evaluations of $f$
- For deterministic or randomized low discrepancy points, error depends on
  integrand variation and point structure; the IID formulas do not apply

::: {.notes}
Exact transport preserves the distribution of $f(\vX)$, so it has the same
IID variance as direct target sampling, though it can be better than weighted
importance sampling for a particular $f$. This does not say that every
change of variables preserves variance: the Keister example changes the
unit-cube integrand, including its Jacobian. The formulas assume finite
second moments and independent replicates or independent antithetic pairs.
:::

## Latin hypercube sampling in one dimension {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="variance-reduction"}

Place one independent uniform point in each of $n$ equal strata:

$$
X_i=\frac{i+U_i}{n},
\qquad U_i\ \IIDsim\ \Unif[0,1],
\qquad i=0,\ldots,n-1
$$

Then $X_i\sim\Unif[i/n,(i+1)/n]$ and

\begin{align*}
\Ex(\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n})
&=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\Ex\{f(X_i)\}\\
&=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\int_{i/n}^{(i+1)/n}f(x)\,\dif x\\
&=\int_0^1f(x)\,\dif x
\end{align*}

The $X_i$ are independent but [not identically distributed]{.alert}

---

### One-dimensional LHS variance

Because the strata are independent,

$$
\var(\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n})
=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\var\{f(X_i)\}
$$

For differentiable $f$, the mean value and Taylor theorems imply

\begin{align*}
\var(\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n})
&\le\frac{\norm{f'}_\infty^2}{n^3},\\
\rmse(\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n})
&\le\frac{\norm{f'}_\infty}{n^{3/2}}
\end{align*}

In one dimension, stratification can improve the IID $n^{-1/2}$ RMSE rate to $n^{-3/2}$ for smooth $f$

---

### Latin hypercube sampling in $d$ dimensions

Let $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_d$ be independent random permutations of $0,\ldots,n-1$:

$$
X_{i\ell}=\frac{\pi_\ell(i)+U_{i\ell}}n,
\qquad U_{i\ell}\ \IIDsim\ \Unif[0,1]
$$

Each point is $\vX_i=(X_{i1},\ldots,X_{id})$; each coordinate uses every stratum exactly once

For $R$ independent Latin hypercubes,

\begin{align*}
\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n}^{(r)}
&=\frac1n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f(\vX_i^{(r)}),\\
\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n,R}
&=\frac1R\sum_{r=1}^R\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n}^{(r)},\\
\widehat{\var}(\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n,R})
&=\frac1{R(R-1)}\sum_{r=1}^R
\left(\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n}^{(r)}-\hmu_{\mathrm{LHS},n,R}\right)^2
\end{align*}

## Comparing random designs {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="variance-low-discrepancy"}

Each design has $n=64$ points in $[0,1]^2$

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-alt: "IID, Latin hypercube, and scrambled Sobol' point sets with 64 points in the unit square"
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| out-width: 96%

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import qmc

plt.rcParams["mathtext.fontset"] = "stix"
n = 64
rng = np.random.default_rng(56504)
designs = {
    "IID": rng.random((n, 2)),
    "Latin hypercube": qmc.LatinHypercube(d=2, seed=56504).random(n),
    "Scrambled Sobol'": qmc.Sobol(d=2, scramble=True, seed=56504).random_base2(6),
}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11.5, 4.2), constrained_layout=True)
for ax, (title, points) in zip(axes, designs.items()):
    ax.scatter(points[:, 0], points[:, 1], s=24, color="#1f5a91", alpha=0.9)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=17)
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$x_1$", fontsize=18, math_fontfamily="stix")
    ax.set_ylabel(r"$x_2$", fontsize=18, math_fontfamily="stix")
    ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=11)
    ax.grid(alpha=0.14)
plt.show()
```

---

### Strengths and limitations of LHS

### Strengths

- No importance density, control variate, or conditional expectation required
- Can converge faster than IID sampling
- Guarantees one point in every one-dimensional stratum

### Limitations

- The sample size is fixed when the design is constructed
- Accuracy assessment requires independent replications
- Too many replications can erase the efficiency gain
- The one-dimensional $n^{-3/2}$ RMSE guarantee does not extend automatically to $d>1$

## The van der Corput sequence {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy-sampling"}

Write a nonnegative integer in base $b$:

$$
i=(\cdots i_2i_1i_0)_b
$$

Reverse the digits across the radix point:

$$
\phi_b(i)=(0.i_0i_1i_2\cdots)_b
=\frac{i_0}b+\frac{i_1}{b^2}+\frac{i_2}{b^3}+\cdots
$$

- Usually $b$ is prime; $b=2$ is common
- $\{\phi_b(i)\}_{i=0}^{b^m-1}$ contains the same points as $\{i/b^m\}_{i=0}^{b^m-1}$ in a different order
- Earlier points keep their order as the sample grows

::: {.key-point}
The van der Corput construction turns a fixed-size grid into an [extensible sequence]{.alert}
:::

---

### First points in base two

For $i=0,1,2,3$, reversing the binary digits gives

$$
\bigl(\phi_2(0),\phi_2(1),\phi_2(2),\phi_2(3)\bigr)
=\bigl(0,\frac12,\frac14,\frac34\bigr)
$$

The first four points form the grid $\{0,1/4,1/2,3/4\}$ in a different order

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Compute $\phi_2(4)$ and $\phi_2(5)$ and identify the two new eighths</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
The new values are $1/8$ and $5/8$, respectively: reverse the three binary
digits in $4=100_2$ and $5=101_2$ across the radix point.
:::

## Four low discrepancy families {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy-sampling"}

For $i=0,1,\ldots$:

| Family | Construction | Typical preferred size |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Kronecker | $\vx_i=i\vzeta\bmod1$ | none |
| Lattice | $\vx_i=\phi_b(i)\vzeta\bmod1$ | $n=b^m$ |
| Halton | $\vx_i=(\phi_2(i),\phi_3(i),\phi_5(i),\ldots)$ | none |
| Digital | $\vx_i=i_0\vc_0\oplus i_1\vc_1\oplus\cdots$ | $n=b^m$ |

Here $\oplus$ denotes digitwise addition modulo $b$

For basic Halton, choosing the coordinate bases fixes the sequence

Different families balance [extensibility]{.alert}, [projection quality]{.alert}, and [fast construction]{.alert}

---

### Lattice sequence: eight points

For the lattice sequence with $b=2$, generator $\vzeta=(1,3)$, and $n=8$,

$$
\vx_i=\phi_2(i)\vzeta\bmod1
$$

| $i$ | $(i)_2$ | $\phi_2(i)$ | $\zeta_1\phi_2(i)\bmod1=x_{i,1}$ | $\zeta_2\phi_2(i)\bmod1=x_{i,2}$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0 | 000 | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| 1 | 001 | $1/2$ | $1/2$ | $1/2$ |
| 2 | 010 | $1/4$ | $1/4$ | $3/4$ |
| 3 | 011 | $3/4$ | $3/4$ | $1/4$ |
| 4 | 100 | $1/8$ | $1/8$ | $3/8$ |
| 5 | 101 | $5/8$ | $5/8$ | $7/8$ |
| 6 | 110 | $3/8$ | $3/8$ | $1/8$ |
| 7 | 111 | $7/8$ | $7/8$ | $5/8$ |

For example, $i=5$ gives $\phi_2(5)=5/8$ and $3(5/8)=15/8\equiv7/8\pmod1$

---

### Kronecker sequence: four points

For hand arithmetic, take $\vzeta=(0.41,0.73)$ and $\vx_i=i\vzeta\bmod1$

| $i$ | $i\zeta_1\bmod1$ | $i\zeta_2\bmod1$ | $\vx_i$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0 | $0$ | $0$ | $(0,0)$ |
| 1 | $0.41$ | $0.73$ | $(0.41,0.73)$ |
| 2 | $0.82$ | $1.46\bmod1=0.46$ | $(0.82,0.46)$ |
| 3 | $1.23\bmod1=0.23$ | $2.19\bmod1=0.19$ | $(0.23,0.19)$ |

The decimal generator keeps this finite example easy to calculate by hand

---

### Digital sequence: four points

In base two, let $i=i_0+2i_1$ and choose
$\vc_0=(1/2,1/2)$, $\vc_1=(1/4,3/4)$

| $i$ | $(i)_2$ | Generators used | $\vx_i=i_0\vc_0\oplus i_1\vc_1$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0 | 00 | none | $(0,0)$ |
| 1 | 01 | $\vc_0$ | $(1/2,1/2)$ |
| 2 | 10 | $\vc_1$ | $(1/4,3/4)$ |
| 3 | 11 | $\vc_0\oplus\vc_1$ | $(3/4,1/4)$ |

For $i=3$, add binary digits **without carrying**:
$(0.10_2,0.10_2)\oplus(0.01_2,0.11_2)=(0.11_2,0.01_2)$

---

### Construct with new generators

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>**Lattice:** Keep $b=2$ and $n=8$, but use $\vzeta=(1,5)$;
find $\vx_4$ and $\vx_5$ using the $\phi_2(i)$ values in the table</span>
:::

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>**Kronecker:** Use $\vzeta=(0.73,0.24)$;
find $\vx_2$ and $\vx_3$ to two decimal places</span>
:::

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>**Digital, $b=2$:** Use $\vc_0=(1/2,1/4)$, $\vc_1=(1/4,1/2)$, and
$\vc_2=(1/8,3/8)$; find $\vx_i$ for $i=0,\ldots,7$</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
Lattice: $\vx_4=(1/8,5/8)$ and $\vx_5=(5/8,1/8)$.
Kronecker: $\vx_2=(0.46,0.48)$ and $\vx_3=(0.19,0.72)$.
These rational decimal generators eventually repeat, unlike the irrational
generators chosen for long Kronecker sequences; here they isolate the hand
calculation of $i\vzeta\bmod1$.
Digital, in order from $i=0$ to $7$:
$(0,0),(1/2,1/4),(1/4,1/2),(3/4,3/4),
(1/8,3/8),(5/8,1/8),(3/8,7/8),(7/8,5/8)$.
The family table does not privilege a particular discrepancy measure;
construction quality depends on the function class and the chosen criterion.
:::

## Randomized low discrepancy sampling {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy-sampling"}

<span id="why-randomize"></span>

Randomization aims for

$$
\vX_{\mathrm{rand},i}\sim\Unif[0,1]^d
$$

for every $i$, while preserving low discrepancy jointly

- [Random shift]{.alert}: $\vX_{\mathrm{rand},i}=\vx_i+\vDelta\bmod1$, especially for lattices and Kronecker sequences
- [Random digital shift]{.alert}: $\vX_{\mathrm{rand},i}=\vx_i\oplus\vDelta$, especially for digital sequences
- [Linear matrix or nested uniform scrambling]{.alert}, especially for digital sequences

Independent randomizations support error assessment without reverting to IID
point placement; recall the [earlier variance and RMSE comparison](#variance-reduction)

::: {.notes}
Each randomized point is marginally uniform, so its sample mean is unbiased.
Randomization almost surely avoids exact cube-boundary points, making Gaussian
quantile transforms finite. The opening variance slide states the nearly
$\Order(n^{-3/2})$ RMSE rate for sufficiently smooth integrands under nested
scrambling.
:::

---

### Shift the points you constructed

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>**Lattice:** For your $\vzeta=(1,5)$ points, suppose the random shift is
$\vDelta=(1/4,1/2)$; find $(\vx_4+\vDelta)\bmod1$ and
$(\vx_5+\vDelta)\bmod1$</span>
:::

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>**Digital, $b=2$:** For your points from $\vc_0,\vc_1,\vc_2$,
suppose the digital shift is $\vDelta=(3/8,1/4)$;
find $\vx_0\oplus\vDelta$ and $\vx_7\oplus\vDelta$</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
Lattice: $\vx_4=(1/8,5/8)$ shifts to $(3/8,1/8)$, and
$\vx_5=(5/8,1/8)$ shifts to $(7/8,5/8)$.
Digital: $\vx_0=(0,0)$ shifts to $(3/8,1/4)$, and
$\vx_7=(7/8,5/8)$ shifts by binary digitwise addition to $(1/2,7/8)$.
The displayed shifts are particular realizations used for hand calculation;
the random shift is uniform on the unit square in the sampling method.
:::

## Component-by-component construction {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="low-discrepancy"}

Generators for lattice rules and digital nets may be chosen by number theory or computer search

The component-by-component strategy:

1. Choose a one-dimensional generator that minimizes a discrepancy criterion over relevant sample sizes
2. Freeze the first $\ell$ components
3. Search for component $\ell+1$ that minimizes discrepancy
4. Increase $\ell$ and repeat until $\ell=d$

::: {.key-point}
A high-dimensional design is built by [optimizing one coordinate at a time]{.alert}
:::

## Stopping criteria {.tree-marker-slide tree-marker="data-driven-error"}

Two practical questions are

\begin{align*}
\abs{\mu-\hmu_n}&\le\text{what?}\\
\abs{\mu-\hmu_n}&\le\varepsilon
\quad\text{for what $n$?}
\end{align*}

We want answers based only on the computed data $f(\vx_0),f(\vx_1),\ldots$

- IID sampling: use a Central Limit Theorem interval when justified
- Randomized low discrepancy sampling: use independent replications
- Deterministic low discrepancy sampling: possible criteria include
  - decay of estimated Fourier coefficients
  - Bayesian credible intervals based on a kernel model

::: {.key-point}
An efficient method needs both [fast error decay]{.alert} and a [reliable stopping rule]{.alert}
:::

# Big Ideas {data-state="goldborder" .tree-marker-slide tree-marker="variance-low-discrepancy"}

- Equivalent expectations can have dramatically different computational variance
- Exact transport chooses a map that makes the target-to-proposal correction
  constant<br>Importance sampling retains the correction as unequal weights
- Importance proposals may be tailored to a particular integrand<br>Transported
  target samples can be reused for many integrands
- Control variates and conditioning remove variability using known structure
- Antithetic sampling and Latin hypercubes introduce useful dependence deliberately
- Low discrepancy sequences replace random clustering with balanced space filling
- Randomization restores unbiasedness and supports error estimation while retaining QMC efficiency

# How Far We Have Come

[A complete path from model to efficient estimate]{.alert}

- [Formulate]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#moments-of-random-variables) — express the target quantity as an expectation
- [Sample]({{< meta decks.d02.file >}}#from-uniformity-to-a-target-distribution) — use direct transforms or Markov chains to represent the target
- [Assess]({{< meta decks.d03.file >}}#discrepancy-as-integration-error) — connect uncertainty and discrepancy to integration error
- [Improve]({{< meta decks.d04.file >}}#variance-reduction) — choose weights, controls, dependence, or low discrepancy points to reduce error

::: {.key-point}
Method choice depends on [error, cost, and a credible stopping rule]{.alert}
:::
